Rust is a general-purpose programming language that emphasizes performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety [1]. It is multi-paradigm, drawing on functional ideas such as immutability, higher-order functions, algebraic data types, and pattern matching [1].

The language began with Graydon Hoare, who started it in 2006 [2]. Mozilla Research sponsored its development from 2009, the first public release came in 2010, and version 1.0 arrived in 2015 [2].

Rust avoids classes and inheritance, offering structs, enums, traits, and methods instead [1]. Its syntax resembles C++, yet it guarantees memory safety without a garbage collector [2].

{"result":"# The Rust Programming Language and Memory Safety

Rust is a general-purpose language that prioritizes performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety [1]. Its multi-paradigm design draws on functional ideas such as immutability, higher-order functions, algebraic data types, and pattern matching [1].

Graydon Hoare began the language in 2006 [2]. Mozilla Research sponsored its development from 2009, the first public release arrived in 2010, and version 1.0 followed in 2015 [2].

Instead of classes and inheritance, Rust offers structs, enums, traits, and methods [1]. Its syntax resembles C++, yet it guarantees memory safety without a garbage collector [2].

Memory safety means being protected from bugs such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers [3]. Java achieves this through runtime checks of array bounds and pointer dereferences [3]. In contrast, C, C++, and Fortran permit arbitrary pointer arithmetic without bounds checking [3].

Rust keeps low-level control while ruling out whole categories of memory errors. Developers who need both speed and safety should therefore weigh it seriously as an option.

### Sources

- [1] [Rust (programming language)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust_%28programming_language%29), Wikipedia
- [2] [Outline of the Rust programming language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outline_of_the_Rust_programming_language), Wikipedia
- [3] [Memory safety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_safety), Wikipedia

{"text":"# The Rust Programming Language and Memory Safety

Rust is a general-purpose language that prioritizes performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety [1]. Its multi-paradigm design draws on functional ideas such as immutability, higher-order functions, algebraic data types, and pattern matching [1].

Graydon Hoare began the language in 2006 [2]. Mozilla Research sponsored its development from 2009, the first public release arrived in 2010, and version 1.0 followed in 2015 [2].

Instead of classes and inheritance, Rust offers structs, enums, traits, and methods [1]. Its syntax resembles C++, yet it guarantees memory safety without a garbage collector [2].

Memory safety means being protected from bugs such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers [3]. Java achieves this through runtime checks of array bounds and pointer dereferences [3]. In contrast, C, C++, and Fortran permit arbitrary pointer arithmetic without bounds checking [3].

Rust keeps low-level control while ruling out whole categories of memory errors. Developers who need both speed and safety should therefore weigh it seriously as an option.","sources":"[1] Wikipedia: Rust (programming language)
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust_%28programming_language%29
Summary: Rust is a general-purpose programming language that emphasizes performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety. Rust supports multiple programming paradigms. It was influenced by ideas from functional programming, including immutability, higher-order functions, algebraic data types, and pattern matching. Rust also provides structs, enums, traits, and methods as alternatives to traditional object-oriented programming, without relying on classes or inheritance.

[2] Wikipedia: Outline of the Rust programming language
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outline_of_the_Rust_programming_language
Summary: The following outline is provided as an overview of and topical guide to Rust: Rust is a multi-paradigm programming language emphasizing performance, memory safety, and concurrency. Rust was initially developed by Graydon Hoare starting in 2006, later sponsored and maintained by Mozilla Research starting in 2009, and first publicly released in 2010, with version 1.0 released in 2015. Rust is syntactically similar to C++ but guarantees memory safety without needing a garbage collector.

[3] Wikipedia: Memory safety
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_safety
Summary: Memory safety is the state of being protected from various software bugs and security vulnerabilities when dealing with memory access, such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers. For example, Java is memory-safe because its runtime error detection checks array bounds and pointer dereferences. By contrast, programming languages like C, C++, and Fortran allow arbitrary pointer arithmetic with pointers implemented as direct memory addresses with no provision for bounds checking, making them memory-unsafe.
